contexts.context: The excerpt highlights several pitfalls when applying automatic differentiation to hybrid or event-driven DAEs. Differentiating through a simulator can produce a gradient tied to the particular computational path chosen by the forward event solver; this is especially fragile when event sequences, switching decisions, or reset branches change. Event handling also introduces derivative contributions from shifts in event time and from reset maps, so ordinary smooth-segment differentiation is incomplete. For DAEs, algebraic variables cannot simply be treated as ordinary differentiated states: they must be re-solved after events and differentiated implicitly while preserving consistency with the algebraic equations. A practical remedy is an AD-through-simulation implementation that differentiates the reduced DAE, implicit algebraic solve, event time, and reset map, while recognizing its local/path-dependent nature. A more controlled alternative is an explicit discrete-adjoint formulation. It retains smooth-segment residuals, event residuals, and event-time stationarity conditions, solving for Lagrange multipliers rather than treating residuals as penalties. This makes the equality constraints and event contributions explicit. The excerpt does not discuss smoothing, straight-through estimators, or randomized smoothing for contacts or switching; instead, it emphasizes exact event residuals, implicit differentiation, consistency restoration, and discrete-adjoint treatment.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports using powder characterization variables as predictors in multivariate models of screw-feeder performance. Material bulk and flow properties can be combined with principal component analysis (PCA) and statistical modeling to quantitatively predict feeding consistency and accuracy, rather than selecting screw geometry solely through trial-and-error feeder experiments. Conditioned bulk density (cBD), used as an indicator of powder packing behavior, showed a correlation with the feed factor—the maximum mass flow rate achievable for a specific material, feeder, and screw combination. Consequently, cBD can be used to estimate the maximum flow for different screw types and to calculate the practical mass-flow operating range once the effective motor-drive range is known. The study tested 14 materials, four screw designs, and six feed rates, identifying an effective drive-command range of approximately 20–90%. Particle size was included among the material characteristics, alongside packing and flow properties, and could therefore contribute to a multivariate relationship describing feeder behavior. The excerpt does not specifically report tapped density or Hausner ratio, but these can represent complementary packing/flow descriptors in a broader model, particularly alongside bulk density and particle-size-distribution metrics. Model outputs could include feed factor, flow-rate consistency, and feeding accuracy, with validation experiments used to confirm predictions for selected material–feeder–screw combinations.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports a multivariate-modeling workflow in which powder material descriptors—such as bulk density, tapped density, Hausner ratio, and particle-size-distribution measures—serve as predictor variables, while experimentally measured feeder responses serve as targets. Fifteen powders were investigated, comprising seven excipients and eight APIs, and were divided into calibration and validation sets. The validation materials were deliberately chosen to exhibit different feeding behavior while having descriptor values within the calibration-set ranges, allowing assessment of model interpolation. For each powder, volumetric feeding tests were conducted at 6, 30, and 54 rpm using a twin-screw feeder. The catch scale provided the raw feed rate, from which feed factor (grams per screw revolution) was calculated and plotted against normalized hopper fill level. Key response variables extracted from these profiles were FFmax, representing maximum material-specific feeding capacity, and FFdecay, representing the hopper-fill level at which feed factor declined to 90% of FFmax. A multivariate model can therefore relate the measured density, flowability, cohesiveness, and particle-size descriptors to FFmax and FFdecay at different screw speeds, enabling prediction of feed rate, feeding stability, and refill-related variability for new powders. The excerpt does not provide the fitted model equations, coefficients, or the individual importance of each material property.

snippets: S1500 (excipient) and API 3 were selected as powders for the validation set since both exhibited a different feeding behavior and the values of their material property descriptors fell within the numerical ranges of the calibration set.
The aim of the volumetric experiments was to obtain a feed factor profile of each powder at each tested screw speed.
FFmax expresses the maximum feeding capacity of a feeder for a specific material and can be used to calculate the maximum achievable feed rate in gravimetric mode.
FFdecay can help to define the hopper refill strategy during gravimetric feeding, thereby reducing the variability induced by a hopper refill.
In total, seven excipients and eight APIs were investigated.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports using powder properties as predictor variables in multivariate models of screw-feeder behavior. A representative database can include density-related, flow-related, particle-size, and other descriptors; the study used 25 material-property descriptors obtained from seven characterization techniques for 15 pharmaceutical powders. Principal component analysis can first identify correlations and reduce or organize the property space, after which partial least-squares (PLS) regression links the selected descriptors to feeder responses. For volumetric feeding, experiments generate feed-factor profiles as a function of hopper fill level, from which maximum feed factor and feed-factor decay are calculated. The excerpt specifically reports that maximum feeding capacity correlates with bulk density and partly with flow properties, while highly compressible, low-density powders may show feed-factor decreases at higher hopper fill levels. For gravimetric feeding, model targets include feed-rate variability (RSD) and the difference between target/setpoint and mean feed rate (RE). Thus, bulk density, tapped-density-related measures, Hausner ratio, and particle-size-distribution descriptors can serve as multivariate inputs, provided they are measured consistently and selected or reduced to avoid redundancy. Model performance should be evaluated by predicting responses for independent validation powders.
contexts.question: How can powder material properties like bulk density, tapped density, Hausner ratio, and particle size distribution be used in multivariate models to predict screw feeder feed factor and feeding performance?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a multivariate modeling strategy in which powder characterization results are used as predictor variables (X) and feeder responses as dependent variables (Y). Bulk density, tapped density, Hausner ratio, and particle-size-distribution measures would therefore be incorporated among the material-property descriptors, alongside other relevant powder characteristics. Partial least squares (PLS) regression is used to manage the potentially correlated descriptors and relate them to screw-feeder performance. For volumetric operation, the principal responses are maximum feed factor (FFmax), representing feeding capacity, and feed-factor decay (FFdecay), indicating how feeding changes with hopper fill level and when refilling may be needed. For gravimetric operation, performance is represented by feed-rate variability (RSD) and the relative error (RE) between the setpoint and mean feed rate. Models are trained using powders with substantially different properties and evaluated by predicting two new powders. According to the excerpt, volumetric responses were predicted more successfully than gravimetric responses because the feeder’s control system compensates for material-property effects in gravimetric mode. In particular, RE showed weak correlation with material properties, while the models were useful for reducing the number of feeding experiments required during process development.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports using measurable powder properties as predictors of feeder behavior, although it does not specifically report a multivariate model containing bulk density, tapped density, Hausner ratio, and particle-size-distribution descriptors. The feeder is volumetric and therefore sensitive to changes in powder packing density. Its outlet balance measures mass flow while piston displacement provides the corresponding powder volume; these measurements are combined into a material-specific “displacement-feed factor” curve. Such curves characterize density variation during feeding and can be used to calibrate the feeder and predict performance at different feed rates. The reported material-property relationships provide a basis for multivariate modeling: particle-size characteristics and compressibility influence whether the powder bed densifies or expands during feeding. Finer particles and more compressible powders tend to densify, whereas larger particles with lower compressibility can exhibit both densification and powder-bed expansion, associated with dilation and elastic recovery. Bulk and tapped density, and consequently Hausner ratio, could therefore serve as quantitative indicators of packing and compressibility, while particle-size-distribution variables capture flow-relevant particle-scale behavior. Together, these predictors could be related statistically to the displacement-feed factor, feed-rate accuracy, and density evolution to predict screw-feeder performance and identify materials requiring calibration.
contexts.question: How can powder material properties like bulk density, tapped density, Hausner ratio, and particle size distribution be used in multivariate models to predict screw feeder feed factor and feeding performance?

contexts.context: The excerpt supports using bulk-density measurements as primary predictors of screw-feeder feed factor, rather than assuming that every powder property contributes equally. Conditioned bulk density (cBD) showed a statistically significant, approximately linear relationship with feed factor for all four screw types, with R-squared values above 0.9 and very small P-values. A model could therefore use cBD, together with screw type, to estimate maximum throughput and define the feasible operating range; the study notes that only about 10 mL of material is needed to obtain cBD. Aerated bulk density and tapped density exhibited similar relationships, but with somewhat weaker R-squared values (approximately 0.75–0.90), so they could be included as alternative or supplementary predictors in a multivariate model. Particle size did not show an identifiable trend in this dataset and should not be treated as a reliable standalone predictor without interactions or additional data. Hausner ratio is not discussed in the excerpt; because it is derived from bulk and tapped density, it could be tested as an engineered predictor of compressibility/flowability, but its incremental value would need validation. Feeding performance should also include drive command, RSD, and RDM: acceptable operation was generally 40–90% drive command, or 20–90% for three screw types.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides the experimental and conceptual basis for using powder properties in multivariate prediction of loss-in-weight feeder behavior, although it does not specifically report models using bulk density, tapped density, Hausner ratio, or particle-size-distribution variables. These material descriptors can be assembled as simultaneous predictors because feeder performance depends strongly on material flow properties. A model would first relate the powder-property vector to the feed factor, obtained during feed-rate calibration; the excerpt defines this initial feed factor as the feeder’s maximum feed rate for the tested powder and tooling. The same predictors could then be used to estimate gravimetric feeding outcomes, such as mass-flow accuracy, consistency, and refill-related deviations, using recorded catch-scale mass and feeder process parameters. Density and Hausner ratio can represent packing and flowability, while particle-size-distribution measures can capture effects associated with cohesion, segregation, and hopper or screw transport. The excerpt also indicates that poor-flowing powders may jam in the hopper or adhere to screw pitches, causing inconsistent mass flow. Thus, multivariate analysis would be appropriate for combining correlated powder-property measurements and identifying their joint relationship with feed factor and feeding performance. However, the excerpt does not provide regression coefficients, validation statistics, or the specific predictive equations.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not present a fitted multivariate model or explicitly define a screw-feeder feed factor, but it identifies the powder descriptors that could serve as model inputs and the feeding responses they may help predict. Bulk (poured) density and tapped density provide information about powder consolidation and packing; their relationship can be used to derive compressibility and Hausner ratio (HR), with higher HR indicating poorer flowability. Particle-size distribution, particularly d50, distinguishes coarse, free-flowing powders from fine, cohesive powders. The examples show CapsuLac60 (d50 = 244 μm, HR = 1.10) as free flowing and GranuLac200 (d50 = 31 μm, HR > 1.22) as poorly flowing. In a multivariate regression or machine-learning model, these variables could be combined—along with interactions such as particle size with density or HR—to predict feed factor, feed rate, and curve shape under specified feeder settings. The reported outcomes suggest that models should account for material-specific density evolution, initial powder-bed expansion, and densification during feeding. Fine powders showed continuously increasing feed rate, whereas di-calcium phosphate and CapsuLac60 exhibited initial expansion followed by densification. Model validation should use repeated feeding experiments because feeding was highly reproducible for a given powder, while constant piston speed produced feed-rate deviations of up to 10–20%.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates how powder properties can be converted into explanatory variables for multivariate prediction of feeder behavior. Particle-size distribution can be represented by dv50, the 50% cumulative undersize of the volumetric particle-size distribution. Density-related predictors include bulk density, calculated from powder mass divided by its initial volume, tapped density, calculated after 1250 taps, and the Hausner ratio, calculated as the ratio of initial to tapped volume. The Carr index and true-density-derived porosity could also be included as related descriptors. These material-property variables can be combined in a multivariate model with operating variables such as screw speed to predict volumetric feeding responses, particularly the maximum feed factor (FFmax) and feed-factor decay (FFdecay), measured at 6, 30, and 54 rpm. The resulting predictions can then be related to gravimetric performance metrics: relative standard deviation (RSD) at feed-rate setpoints of 0.1 and 0.55 kg/h, and relative error (RE) at those same setpoints. In this framework, density and particle size serve as candidate predictors of powder packing, consolidation, and flow, while FFmax, FFdecay, RSD, and RE are response variables. However, this excerpt describes the measurements and response definitions rather than the fitted model coefficients or the direction and strength of individual property effects.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies bulk density, tapped density, Hausner ratio, and particle-size distribution as measurable raw-material descriptors that can serve as input variables in multivariate models of powder feeding. Particle-size distribution can be represented by the 50% cumulative undersize of the volumetric distribution (dv50), while bulk and tapped density can be combined into the Hausner ratio, providing an indicator of powder flow and compressibility. Together with other descriptors such as Carr index, true density, porosity, and ring-shear flow properties, these variables can be used to relate powder characteristics to screw-feeder outcomes such as feed factor and overall feeding performance. In practice, a fitted multivariate model would use the measured property values to estimate the expected feed factor and identify which material attributes most strongly influence feeding behavior. The excerpt indicates that the models used in the study assume linear relationships, so their predictive performance may be limited when powder properties interact nonlinearly. Expanding the powder database and investigating nonlinear modeling approaches were proposed as ways to improve prediction. Such models could reduce the number of feeding experiments required during process development, making development of new drug products faster and more efficient. The provided pages do not report specific coefficients or the relative importance of each listed property.

contexts.context: For simultaneous state and parameter estimation, the joint UKF (JUKF) augments the state vector by concatenating the system states and unknown parameters, then uses a single UKF to propagate and update them together. This structure directly represents the cross-covariance between state and parameter estimates, allowing their statistical dependence to be included in the update. Its principal trade-off is computational cost: the augmented vector is larger, so more sigma points must be generated and propagated, and a full covariance matrix—including state-parameter and parameter-parameter terms—must be handled. The dual UKF (DUKF) decouples the two estimation tasks and uses two simultaneous filters: one estimates parameters and the other estimates states. The parameter filter’s output is supplied as input to the state filter. This separation can reduce the burden associated with an augmented filter and avoids directly maintaining the full joint state-parameter covariance, but it also treats the estimation processes as separate rather than representing their cross-covariance in one augmented filter. The excerpt therefore characterizes JUKF as more integrated but potentially more expensive, while DUKF is structurally decoupled and computationally attractive, with the parameter-to-state information passed through the filter input.
contexts.question: How do dual UKF and joint UKF work for simultaneous state and parameter estimation? What are the trade-offs between joint filtering and dual filtering approaches?

contexts.context: The excerpt frames dual and joint unscented Kalman filtering as UKF/UF replacements for corresponding EKF-based approaches in simultaneous state and model-parameter estimation. In dual filtering, two estimators are maintained: one estimates the dynamic state using the current parameter or weight estimate, while the other estimates parameters using the current state estimate. This separation is modular and follows the alternating structure described for the dual EKF. In joint filtering, the state and parameters are concatenated into one augmented state vector and a single filter estimates them together, allowing their uncertainty and interactions to be represented within the combined covariance. The UKF performs the nonlinear prediction and update through sigma points and weighted transformed statistics rather than local Taylor linearization. The excerpt claims third-order accuracy for Gaussian inputs and says that Jacobians and Hessians are unnecessary. Thus, joint filtering offers a unified treatment of state-parameter coupling but operates on a larger augmented dimension, whereas dual filtering uses separate, smaller estimation problems and is easier to organize modularly, at the cost of relying on alternating current estimates rather than one jointly represented state. The passage does not provide a detailed empirical comparison of these trade-offs.

In a joint approach, states and parameters are combined into one augmented state representation and propagated together through a nonlinear filter; the text explicitly identifies joint-EKF and joint-UKF as methods obtained using this concept. contexts.context: The excerpt describes the basic distinction between joint and dual estimation, although it explicitly illustrates the dual approach with EKFs rather than a complete dual-UKF derivation. In joint filtering, unknown parameters are augmented into the state vector, so one nonlinear filter estimates the physical states and parameters together. This creates a unified state-space model and allows the state–parameter correlations to be represented directly. A joint-UKF applies the unscented transform to this augmented vector, propagating sigma points through the nonlinear dynamics and measurement equations; it is generally more accurate than EKF-based linearization when the system is strongly nonlinear, though the excerpt notes that UKF estimates remain approximate and can contain systematic higher-order error. In dual filtering, two filters operate simultaneously: one estimates the states and the other estimates the unknown parameters, with the filters exchanging relevant estimates. This separation can reduce matrix dimensions and computational burden, particularly for inverse-matrix calculations, and may be attractive for large models. The trade-off is weaker coupling between state and parameter estimates: the excerpt reports that dual-EKF convergence is less likely than joint-EKF convergence. Joint filtering therefore offers stronger coupled estimation and potentially better convergence, but at the cost of a larger augmented covariance and greater computational complexity.
contexts.question: How do dual UKF and joint UKF work for simultaneous state and parameter estimation? What are the trade-offs between joint filtering and dual filtering approaches?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes two ways to estimate a nonlinear signal state and model parameters simultaneously using unscented filtering. In dual filtering, separate filters are maintained for the signal state and the parameter/weight vector. The parameter vector is modeled as a stationary or random-walk state, while the noisy signal observation is rewritten as a measurement for the parameter filter. At each time step, the current parameter estimate drives the signal filter, and the current signal estimate drives the parameter filter. A dual UF replaces the EKF in both filters; a dual UF/EKF uses the unscented filter for the signal and an EKF for parameter estimation. In joint filtering, the signal state and parameter vector are concatenated into one augmented state, and a single recursive UF (joint UF) estimates them together. The excerpt identifies the main conceptual trade-off: dual filtering separates the estimation tasks and allows different filters or approximations for each, whereas joint filtering directly represents their combined distribution and correlations in one state. Experimental results favor UT-based methods, particularly dual UF, with lower estimation and prediction errors and more stable learning curves than the corresponding EKF methods. The excerpt does not provide detailed computational or covariance-complexity comparisons between dual and joint filtering.

In the joint formulation, states and unknown parameters are handled together: the initial covariance matrix contains both state and parameter uncertainties, while MJUKF separates parameter covariance into a dedicated vector, pθ. contexts.context: The excerpt describes two Kalman-filter strategies for simultaneously estimating dynamic states and unknown parameters, applicable within either extended or unscented Kalman filter frameworks. Joint UKF augments the state vector with the parameters and estimates this combined vector using one filter recursion. Its principal advantage is that the augmented covariance explicitly represents state–parameter cross-dependencies, making it preferable when such correlations are important. Its cost is a larger augmented state and a single, more computationally demanding filter. Dual UKF instead runs two parallel filters: a state filter and a parameter filter. At each time step, the parameter estimates are treated as known by the state filter, while the state estimates are treated as known by the parameter filter. This separates the estimation tasks and requires two filters, but it does not explicitly estimate cross-covariance terms, effectively assuming those terms are zero. The excerpt notes that switching the state and parameter estimates between filters while using the same measurements can implicitly impose a constraint and may develop cross-covariance effects. Consequently, despite the theoretical distinction, reported experiments found little difference between joint and dual approaches. The trade-off is therefore explicit dependence modeling and unified estimation in the joint method versus simpler partitioned filtering in the dual method.
contexts.question: How do dual UKF and joint UKF work for simultaneous state and parameter estimation? What are the trade-offs between joint filtering and dual filtering approaches?

contexts.context: The excerpt contrasts two UKF-based strategies for jointly estimating system states and parameters. In a dual UKF, state and parameter estimation are separated into distinct filters; each filter treats the variable handled by the other as constant. This separation means the state–parameter cross-covariance is set to zero or not computed. Consequently, dual filtering does not capture correlations between states and parameters, which can reduce estimation effectiveness when those quantities are coupled. In a joint UKF (JUKF), the parameter vector is concatenated with the state vector to form an augmented state. A single UKF then generates sigma points for this combined vector, propagates them through the nonlinear state and measurement models, and updates both states and parameters using their joint covariance, including state–parameter cross-covariance. This generally offers more effective parameter estimation because the coupling is represented explicitly. The principal trade-off is computational cost: the augmented dimension increases the number of sigma points and makes sigma-point generation—identified as the most expensive UKF operation—more costly. The article therefore motivates a modified JUKF that creates separate parameter sigma points to reduce the standard JUKF’s computational complexity while preserving parameter convergence, particularly where a suitable linear measurement–parameter transformation exists.

contexts.context: Profile likelihood assesses identifiability by selecting one parameter, scanning it across a range of values, and re-optimizing all remaining parameters at every fixed value. This produces a profile likelihood curve that follows the best-fitting compensation path through parameter space, rather than relying only on local curvature at the optimum. The confidence interval consists of parameter values whose profile remains below the likelihood threshold L(ŷ) + χ²α,1; a finite, confined interval indicates practical identifiability, while an interval extending toward a parameter boundary indicates non-identifiability. Re-optimization reveals parameter compensation: if other parameters can adjust to preserve a similarly good fit, the profile stays relatively flat or may show asymmetric, non-quadratic behavior. Such shapes expose nonlinear parameter relationships and sloppiness that Fisher-information or local Hessian methods can miss. A profile that remains constant over arbitrary values indicates structural non-identifiability, generally caused by over-parameterization and model symmetries. The excerpt explicitly supports these identifiability and compensation diagnostics, but it does not fully explain how profile likelihood distinguishes structural model error from parameter non-identifiability; that requires examining systematic profile deviations, poor fit, or residual patterns in conjunction with model criticism.
contexts.question: How does profile likelihood work for assessing practical identifiability of parameters? How does it detect parameter compensation, structural model error, and sloppiness?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes profile-likelihood assessment through the likelihood (represented by χ²): parameters are fitted by minimizing χ², and confidence limits are obtained by examining how far χ² increases from its minimum before reaching a chosen threshold α. A parameter is practically identifiable when this interval is finite. Practical non-identifiability can occur even when the likelihood has a unique optimum: a profile may remain sufficiently flat in one direction that a confidence bound is infinite. In parameter space this appears as an extended, shallow valley, indicating that different parameter combinations produce observables that change only negligibly relative to measurement accuracy. Such movement along the valley represents parameter compensation. Structural non-identifiability is distinguished by an exactly flat, infinitely extended manifold generated by a functional relation among parameters; the observables and χ² remain unchanged, so the parameters cannot be estimated uniquely. Practical non-identifiability instead reflects limited or noisy data and may have one finite and one infinite confidence bound. The excerpt also notes that internal states can vary strongly along a practically non-identifiable direction despite nearly unchanged observables. Thus, profile likelihood reveals sloppiness through flat or weakly curved profiles and can expose compensation or structural ambiguity through extended likelihood valleys. Specific procedures for diagnosing structural model error are not provided in this excerpt.
contexts.question: How does profile likelihood work for assessing practical identifiability of parameters? How does it detect parameter compensation, structural model error, and sloppiness?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes profile likelihood as a method for assessing practical, rather than structural, identifiability with finite noisy and incomplete data. First, the full mechanistic-plus-measurement-error model is fitted by maximum likelihood, producing the MLE and a normalized log-likelihood whose maximum is zero. The parameter vector is partitioned into a parameter of interest ψ and nuisance parameters λ. For each fixed value of ψ across a chosen mesh, the normalized log-likelihood is re-optimized over λ; the resulting supremum is the profile log-likelihood. Thus, the profile traces the best achievable fit for every constrained value of ψ, while implicitly recording compensating optimal nuisance-parameter values λ*(ψ). A sharply peaked profile indicates that the data constrain ψ near the MLE, whereas a broad, flat, or weakly bounded profile indicates poor practical identifiability and parameter sloppiness. The excerpt does not explicitly explain how to diagnose structural model error. More generally, parameter compensation would appear through substantial changes in λ*(ψ) that preserve a similarly high likelihood, revealing trade-offs among parameters. Structural model error cannot be distinguished solely from parameter non-identifiability by the procedure described; it would require examining systematic lack of fit or additional model diagnostics.

contexts.context: Profile likelihood assesses a parameter by varying it across a range around the maximum-likelihood estimate while repeatedly re-optimizing all other parameters. The resulting profile shows how much the fit worsens as the parameter changes, and confidence thresholds determine whether a finite confidence interval can be obtained. A structurally non-identifiable parameter produces a completely flat profile: the fit remains unchanged over the explored range, yielding an infinite confidence interval. This indicates that changes in the profiled parameter can be compensated by changes in other parameters. The compensating parameters can be identified by plotting their fitted values along the profile; coupled parameter trajectories reveal the parameter combinations responsible for the non-identifiability. Practical non-identifiability instead appears when the profile remains below the confidence threshold over a very broad or one-sided range, such as an infinite extension toward lower parameter values, although a finite bound may exist in the other direction. Thus, profile likelihood reveals weakly constrained or sloppy parameter directions through broad, shallow profiles and large confidence intervals. The excerpt does not explain how profile likelihood specifically detects structural model error; it only describes structural non-identifiability, parameter compensation, and practical non-identifiability. It also notes that calculating profiles can be computationally demanding because of repeated numerical re-optimization.
contexts.question: How does profile likelihood work for assessing practical identifiability of parameters? How does it detect parameter compensation, structural model error, and sloppiness?

contexts.context: Dynamax is an open-source Python package for probabilistic state space modeling built on JAX. It combines functionally pure, low-level inference routines with high-level objects for constructing, fitting, and inspecting state space models. Differentiating this likelihood with respect to transition, emission, noise, and initial-state parameters yields gradients that can be supplied to gradient-based optimizers, enabling maximum-likelihood parameter learning. contexts.context: The excerpt describes autodifferentiable ensemble Kalman filters (AD-EnKFs), rather than Dynamax specifically or the standard Kalman-filter marginal likelihood. AD-EnKFs combine ensemble Kalman filtering for sequential state estimation with automatic differentiation for learning unknown dynamics. They support parametric models with unknown parameters, neural-network surrogate dynamics, and partially known models augmented by neural-network corrections. Parameter learning proceeds by running the EnKF to obtain an estimate of the data log-likelihood, differentiating that estimated likelihood with respect to the dynamics parameters, and taking a gradient-ascent step. Crucially, differentiation accounts for both the explicit parameter dependence of the likelihood and the dependence of the EnKF-generated particles on the parameters. The reparameterization trick makes this computational graph differentiable in software such as PyTorch, JAX, and TensorFlow. In a conventional state-space model with a differentiable Kalman filter, the analogous idea is to differentiate the exact marginal likelihood computed through the prediction-error decomposition: each time step contributes an innovation residual and its covariance, and automatic differentiation propagates through the prediction, update, and likelihood calculations to obtain gradients for maximum-likelihood optimization. The excerpt contrasts this with EM-EnKF methods, which hold the generated particles fixed and therefore omit gradients through the particle-generation process.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not mention Dynamax explicitly, nor does it provide the standard Kalman-filter prediction-error decomposition in detail. It does, however, describe autodifferentiable ensemble Kalman filters (AD-EnKF), which are a related approach: the entire EnKF computation is treated as a differentiable map from model parameters θ to an estimated data log-likelihood. Because the ensemble particles are regarded as functions of θ, automatic differentiation can produce gradients of the estimated likelihood with respect to parameters governing the dynamics, observation model, or noise statistics. These gradients can then support gradient-based parameter learning in state-space models, in contrast to EM-style methods that do not differentiate through the EnKF itself. The paper establishes convergence guarantees for EnKF log-likelihood gradients in linear-Gaussian settings and reports improved likelihood and gradient estimation over particle-filter methods in high-dimensional systems. It also emphasizes localization and truncated backpropagation through time for long sequences. For a conventional Kalman filter, the analogous idea is to differentiate the sum of sequential innovation log-density terms produced by prediction and update steps; this excerpt supports the broader differentiable-filtering principle, but not the exact Kalman equations or Dynamax API.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not mention Dynamax, so it provides no definition of that software package or library. It does describe the central idea behind autodifferentiable Kalman filtering, specifically an autodifferentiable ensemble Kalman filter (AD-EnKF). The model is a state-space system with parameterized transition dynamics Fα and process-noise covariance Qβ, while the observation matrix and observation-noise covariance are assumed known. Filtering alternates between forecast and analysis steps. Each filtering update contributes a normalizing constant Zt(θ), equal to the predictive observation likelihood pθ(yt|y1:t−1). Consequently, the full data log-likelihood is decomposed into a sum of log predictive likelihoods: L(θ)=Σt log Zt(θ). In nonlinear or otherwise non-Gaussian settings, these quantities can be approximated using an ensemble of particles and empirical forecast moments. Because the particles, covariance estimates, Kalman gains, and likelihood estimate depend on θ, the resulting EnKF likelihood map can be differentiated automatically. Its gradient can then be used with gradient ascent to learn unknown dynamical parameters, process-noise parameters, neural-network surrogate dynamics, or model-correction terms. After learning, the fitted transition kernel can be used for state recovery through filtering.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to differentiable Kalman filtering but does not mention Dynamax by name or explain the Kalman-filter marginal likelihood/prediction-error decomposition in detail. It describes differentiable filtering as embedding Kalman-style recursive state estimation in a gradient-based learning framework. Such methods can learn system dynamics, observation models, uncertainty models, or correction terms directly from data while retaining the structure and interpretability of filtering algorithms. The excerpt distinguishes several approaches: DEKF, DUKF, DEnKF, and differentiable particle filters, noting their differing abilities to handle nonlinearity, high-dimensional systems, and end-to-end gradients. The proposed DKF uses an adjoint-based two-level optimization procedure: a field-inversion step identifies discrepancies between approximate and true dynamics, and a closure model is then trained to represent those discrepancies. Its claimed advantages include support for nonlinear and high-dimensional problems, end-to-end gradients, scalability, and improved state reconstruction. These ideas provide context for learning state-space-model parameters by differentiating through the filtering computation, but the supplied pages do not specify the prediction-error likelihood formula, gradients of the marginal likelihood, or an implementation such as Dynamax.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Context: we are building an open-source, low-cost powder doser for gravimetric dosing of dry powders (salt as the development surrogate; ultimately metal additive-manufacturing feedstocks such as AlSi10Mg, plus food/pharma powders) inside a self-driving-lab loop. Hardware: an Archimedean auger in a tube driven by a stepper motor (44:20 gear), a solenoid tapper that strikes the tube, and a servo that tilts the whole assembly (0-70 degrees), dispensing into a cup on an A&D HR-100A analytical balance (102 g capacity, 0.1 mg readability). The balance is mechanically isolated from the doser; at its factory response setting it emits a new datum only every ~197 ms (5.1 Hz), and drop-weight step tests show a first-order response with time constant tau_bal ~ 0.16 s (R^2 > 0.995, independent of mass and drop height).

Current controller ("bang-bang" bulk + trim): dispense at full rate while a 3-state Kalman filter (true cup mass m, deposition rate r, lagged balance reading b; the balance observes b) runs on the balance stream; halt the auger when the predicted settled mass m_hat + AF0 + tau_af * r_hat (+ k * sigma) reaches target minus a guard; then a slow increment/tap trim closes the remaining tens of mg on settled readings. Two per-powder quantities dominate this predictor:

(1) FEED FACTOR phi (g per auger revolution, i.e. the volumetric-feeder "feed factor"). For salt it is ~0.14-0.23 g/rev at working tilts; across 8 powders (salt, calcium lactate, AlSi10Mg, xanthan gum, rice flours, sodium alginate, CMC) it spans <0.03 to ~0.23 g/rev. # Data Assimilation and Parameter Estimation for a Low-Cost Powder Doser: A Literature-Grounded Technical Assessment

## Q1. Whitehead's Research and What Transfers

### 1a. Continuous Data Assimilation and Parameter Learning

Jared P. Whitehead's data-assimilation research centers on the Carlson–Hudson–Larios (CHL) algorithm and its extensions, which learn unknown parameters of a chaotic system online from partial observations. The CHL method augments the Azouani–Olson–Titi (AOT) nudging framework: a model copy is continuously nudged toward observed data through a feedback-control term, and the residual error that remains when parameters are incorrect provides the signal for parameter recovery (carlson2108dynamicallylearningthe pages 2-4). Specifically, when parameters are correct and nudging is sufficiently strong, the assimilated state synchronizes with the true state; with incorrect parameters, a persistent finite error remains, and that error supplies the updating direction (carlson2108dynamicallylearningthe pages 6-8). For the Lorenz system, convergence to the correct parameters is proven under conditions of dissipativity (bounded absorbing-ball dynamics), sufficiently large nudging gains, and a non-degeneracy condition requiring that the observed-state mismatch remain informative at update times (carlson2108dynamicallylearningthe pages 6-8).

Pachev, Whitehead, and McQuarrie (2022) extended CHL to concurrent multi-parameter learning on the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation. Their framework uses an orthogonality condition that cancels the residual forcing in the observable-error equation, yielding exponential decay of the observable error at rate μ. For multiple parameters, this single equation is underdetermined, so additional constraints or sensitivity directions are required. Observation density is encoded by an interpolation operator I_h, with smaller h corresponding to resolving more relevant scales (pachev2022concurrentmultiparameterlearninga pages 3-5, pachev2022concurrentmultiparameterlearning pages 3-5).

Newey, Whitehead, and Carlson (2025) recast the CHL update as Newton's method applied to the long-time assimilation error E(c) = ½||I_h(v(c)−u)||². They showed that Levenberg–Marquardt (LM) performs similarly to CHL/Newton for a single parameter but generalizes much better to multiple parameters, reducing the error by a factor of three in multi-parameter experiments on modified KSE (newey2025modeldiscoveryon pages 24-29, newey2025modeldiscoveryon pages 9-13). The LM regularization (W^T W + λI)^{−1} stabilizes ill-conditioned or poorly identifiable directions (newey2025modeldiscoveryon pages 13-19). The paper uses a single real-time simulation and updates parameters as data arrive, contrasting with ensemble or batch methods (newey2025modeldiscoveryon pages 1-5). However, direct comparisons with stochastic/ensemble methods are not provided in the paper; these are mentioned only as future directions (newey2025modeldiscoveryon pages 24-29).

**Assumptions that survive translation to this rig:**

- *Dissipativity*: The powder doser's cup-mass dynamics are bounded and dissipative (mass accumulates monotonically up to a target; balance lag decays exponentially). This assumption holds naturally.
- *Observation density*: The 5 Hz balance stream observes a single scalar with ~0.16 s lag. This is far sparser than "continuous observation of multiple state components." CHL's convergence proofs assume access to enough observed components to enforce synchronization; with one lagged scalar, the nudging gain cannot directly enforce synchronization of unobserved states (screw inventory, lip reservoir, in-flight mass).
- *Synchronization*: The hybrid start/stop dynamics and threshold-triggered halts break continuous-time flow. The CHL "relax then punch" strategy requires the model to settle to a quasi-steady mismatch between parameter updates, but the powder doser's operational runs last only 30–120 s with abrupt state changes (newey2025modeldiscoveryon pages 5-9).
- *Non-degeneracy*: For afterflow parameters to be identifiable via CHL, the observed error must carry information about AF₀ and τ_af, which it does only at halt events—not during continuous flow.

**Verdict**: The CHL/LM framework's most transferable insight is that a deterministic optimizer operating on a long-time mismatch functional provides a computationally cheap, derivative-based alternative to ensemble methods. However, the single-scalar, lagged, 5 Hz observation, short run duration, and hybrid dynamics mean that the formal synchronization and convergence guarantees do not apply. LM's regularization of ill-conditioned multi-parameter directions is directly useful for the proposed MAP fit.

### 1b. Bayesian Inversion in Small-Data, High-Uncertainty Settings

Whitehead's tsunami work (Ringer et al. 2021; Paskett et al. 2024; Wonnacott et al. 2024) demonstrates Bayesian inversion for estimating earthquake or landslide parameters from sparse, uncertain historical observations using expensive forward models. The framework assigns prior distributions informed by expert knowledge and instrumental records, constructs observation likelihoods from uncertain anecdotal accounts (wave arrival times, heights, inundation lengths) with explicitly modeled error distributions (skew-normal, normal), and samples the posterior via random-walk Metropolis–Hastings MCMC over 200,000+ forward simulations (ringer2021methodologicalreconstructionof pages 1-2, wonnacott2024methodologicalreconstructionof pages 7-9, paskett2024ataleof pages 3-5). The open-source `tsunamibayes` Python package implements this pipeline and is designed so that assumptions can be changed directly in code (ringer2021methodologicalreconstructionof pages 1-2).

Key methodological features that transfer:

- **Explicit uncertainty modeling**: Each observation type gets its own distributional model rather than assuming additive Gaussian noise everywhere. For the doser, this supports using Student-t or mixture likelihoods for slug/clump arrivals.
- **Low-dimensional parameterization**: The tsunami studies deliberately keep parameter spaces small (6–9 parameters) to make MCMC tractable with expensive forward models (ringer2021methodologicalreconstructionof pages 4-7, paskett2024ataleof pages 1-3). The doser's 3–5 parameters are well within this range.
- **Prior construction from sparse evidence**: Landslide priors are built from only 25 published events (wonnacott2024methodologicalreconstructionof pages 5-7). Similarly, per-powder priors can be constructed from a handful of calibration sessions.
- **Model comparison**: Paskett et al. (2024) compare competing fault hypotheses via posterior support (paskett2024ataleof pages 1-3), directly applicable to comparing constant vs. history-dependent afterflow models.

**Assumptions that differ**: The tsunami forward model is deterministic (shallow-water PDE), continuous, and expensive (~minutes per evaluation). The doser model is cheap (~ms), stochastic (granular clumps), and discontinuous (start/stop events). These differences favor full posterior sampling for the doser more than for the tsunami problem, since forward evaluations are trivially cheap.

## Q2. Method Fit: Comparing Estimation Approaches

### MAP with Autodiff and a Gaussian Prior as 4D-Var

A single-run MAP fit with automatic differentiation through a deterministic simulator, penalized by a Gaussian prior on parameters, is mathematically equivalent to strong-constraint 4D-Var with a background term (ebtehaj2013onvariationaldownscaling pages 20-22, frion2026addaamodular pages 4-5). The 4D-Var cost function combines a background/prior term ||θ − θ_b||²_{B⁻¹} (which is Tikhonov regularization with the prior covariance B as the regularization operator) with accumulated observation misfits over the assimilation window (ebtehaj2014variationaldataassimilation pages 3-6, freitag2013synergyofinverse pages 1-4). If process noise or model-error terms are added as additional unknowns, the formulation becomes weak-constraint 4D-Var (frion2026addaamodular pages 4-5).

The Laplace approximation—approximating the posterior as Gaussian centered on the MAP estimate with covariance given by the inverse Hessian—is adequate when the posterior is unimodal and approximately quadratic. For a 30–120 s run with only 2–4 parameters, this is often reasonable but must be verified. Under Gaussian error assumptions, MAP and the posterior mean coincide for linear problems, but nonlinear dynamics generally produce non-Gaussian posteriors (frion2026addaamodular pages 4-5, lorenc2003modellingoferror pages 12-14). Profile likelihood analysis provides a practical check: if profiles are approximately parabolic, the Laplace approximation is adequate; if they are asymmetric, flat, or boundary-seeking, it is not (maiwald2016drivingthemodel pages 5-7, raue2009structuralandpractical pages 2-3).

### Recommendation

For a single 30–120 s calibration run, the **differentiable Kalman-filter marginal likelihood** (prediction-error method) is the strongest first production estimator. It analytically integrates out latent states (cup mass, rate, balance lag), respects the stochastic nature of powder arrivals through process noise, and produces a likelihood that can be differentiated end-to-end with JAX for MAP optimization (linderman2025dynamaxapython pages 1-2, chen2022autodifferentiableensemblekalman pages 5-7). The resulting Hessian or profile-likelihood intervals provide initial uncertainty quantification, while offline HMC/NUTS sampling of selected sessions serves as a validation benchmark for the Laplace approximation. The dual/augmented UKF remains the method of choice for real-time within-dose control but should estimate at most one parameter (φ) online, treating afterflow parameters as fixed from the latest calibration (onat2019anoveland pages 1-2, gove2006applicationofa pages 5-7).

## Q3. Identifiability and Experimental Design of the Calibration Run

### Observability Structure

The feed factor φ is observable from any flowing segment: the balance accumulation rate during flow is approximately φ × (RPM), so multiple seconds of steady flow at known speed suffice. The afterflow parameters (AF₀, τ_af) are observable only at halts, and the data show that afterflow also depends on run duration and lip/screw inventory, meaning these are not pure stop-response parameters. With one scalar sensor at 5 Hz, the Fisher information matrix for (φ, AF₀, τ_af) jointly will be rank-deficient unless the calibration run includes multiple halts at different flow conditions.

### Profile Likelihood for Identifiability Assessment

Profile likelihood is the recommended primary identifiability diagnostic. For each parameter of interest, it is varied across a range while all other parameters are re-optimized, producing a curve that reveals practical identifiability (finite confidence interval), structural non-identifiability (flat profile), or parameter compensation (coupled parameter changes that preserve fit quality) (maiwald2016drivingthemodel pages 5-7, wieland2021onstructuraland pages 4-7, raue2009structuralandpractical pages 2-3). Flat or weakly bounded profiles expose sloppy parameter directions that local Hessian methods miss (maiwald2016drivingthemodel pages 2-3). Profile likelihood also reveals when parameters are compensating for structural model error rather than measuring something physical: if the compensating parameter trajectory along the profile is physically implausible or if residual patterns change systematically, the model is absorbing misspecification (murphy2024implementingmeasurementerror pages 9-11).

### Designing the Single Calibration Run

Based on Fisher-information and D-optimal design principles (ayres2609parameteridentifiabilityof pages 20-21, ayres2609parameteridentifiabilityof pages 9-12), the calibration run should:

1. **Include 6–10 start-stop segments** to provide multiple independent afterflow observations. Each halt is essentially one "experiment" for (AF₀, τ_af); with only 2–3 halts, these parameters will be practically non-identifiable.
2. **Use at least 3 RPM levels** (e.g., 15, 45, 75 rpm) to separate φ from RPM-dependent effects and to span the afterflow model A = AF₀ + τ_af × flow.
3. **Vary segment durations deliberately** (some short, ~2–5 s; some long, ~15–30 s) to expose the history/lip-inventory dependence identified in the data.
4. **Hold tilt and tapping fixed** in the first protocol to reduce the parameter count. Only add tilt variation after the base model is identifiable.
5. **Use commanded stops** (not threshold-triggered) so the halt timing is a known input rather than a stochastic function of the estimated state.
6. **Allow ≥ 1 s of settled balance readings** after each halt before restarting, to cleanly observe the afterflow transient.

### Number of Concurrent Parameters

With this design, 2–3 parameters (φ, AF₀, and optionally τ_af) can realistically be estimated concurrently. Adding a fourth parameter (e.g., a lip-inventory decay constant) risks producing sloppy, compensating combinations. The sloppiness diagnostic is the eigenvalue spectrum of the Fisher information matrix or the Hessian at the MAP: if eigenvalues span several orders of magnitude (log-uniformly spaced), the model is sloppy and only stiff combinations are constrained by data (maiwald2016drivingthemodel pages 5-7). In systems biology, this is ubiquitous and is addressed by reparameterizing to stiff eigenvector combinations or by fixing sloppy directions at prior values.

### Detecting Compensation for Model Error

If τ_af varies substantially between datasets (as observed: 0.28 s to 1.07 s), this signals that the linear afterflow model A = AF₀ + τ_af × flow is absorbing history-dependent or nonlinear effects. The profile likelihood of τ_af will be broad, and the compensating parameter trajectories will show AF₀ and τ_af trading off. The remedy is either to extend the model (add a history-dependent reservoir term) or to accept that afterflow is described by a per-run effective value rather than a material constant.

## Q4. Priors, Drift, and Storage

### Setting and Inflating Prior Variance

The stored per-powder parameter estimates should be treated as priors for subsequent sessions, not constants. Several approaches to specifying and inflating prior variance are relevant:

**Random-walk parameter models**: The simplest approach models log(φ) as a random walk with variance growing linearly with elapsed time or dispensed mass: Var(log φ_{t+Δt}) = Var(log φ_t) + σ²_drift · Δt. The drift variance σ²_drift can be estimated empirically from replicated sessions. Time-varying parameter models with random-walk evolution are standard in econometrics and signal processing (onat2019anoveland pages 1-2).

**Hierarchical Bayesian models**: With multiple powders and sessions, a hierarchical structure population → powder → lot → session decomposes the total variance. Population-level hyperparameters encode "typical" feed-factor range and typical session-to-session drift for any powder; powder-level parameters capture material-specific means; session-level parameters capture the current operating conditions. This is the natural long-term architecture but requires data from multiple powders and sessions before the hierarchy is estimable.

**Empirical Bayes across a multi-powder database**: After accumulating calibration records from many powders, the population-level distribution can be estimated and used as an informative prior for a new, uncharacterized powder. This is analogous to the tsunami work's use of published landslide measurements to construct empirically informed priors (wonnacott2024methodologicalreconstructionof pages 5-7).

**Material-property-predicted priors**: Multivariate models using PLS regression can predict feed factor from measured powder properties. Bostijn et al. (2019) used 25 material-property descriptors (including bulk density, tapped density, Hausner ratio, d_v50, compressibility) to predict maximum feed factor (FF_max) and feed-factor decay with fill level (FF_decay) for a twin-screw feeder (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 6-10, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 1-6, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 14-18). Li (2020) showed that conditioned bulk density alone has R² > 0.9 with feed factor across four screw types (li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 49-53). These predictions can serve as physics-informed prior means, with the prediction residual variance as the prior variance, for a new powder whose material properties are measured but whose feeder behavior is unknown.

### Why Feed Factor Drifts 1.5–2× for the Same Material

The screw-feeder and loss-in-weight feeder literature identifies several mechanisms:

1. **Hopper fill level and head pressure**: As powder is discharged, the head pressure at the screw inlet decreases, altering how consistently screw flights fill. In funnel-flow hoppers, outlet stress decreases continuously with fill level, producing a characteristic feed-factor decay curve. In mass-flow hoppers, outlet stress remains more constant (fathollahi2024improvingcontinuouslossinweight pages 1-2, fathollahi2024improvingcontinuouslossinweight pages 2-4).

2. **Powder consolidation and densification**: Compressible powders densify under their own weight over time. Since the screw transports a fixed volume per revolution, increased density means increased mass per revolution (higher feed factor). Conversely, aeration from disturbance can temporarily lower density and feed factor (li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 66-73, li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 1-8).

3. **Refill events**: In loss-in-weight feeders, hopper refilling can compress the existing powder bed, forcing excess material into screw flights and producing overfeeding. Refill-induced disturbances are the largest documented source of feed-rate deviation (li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 66-73, engisch2014lossinweightfeedingin pages 134-139, engisch2014lossinweightfeedingin pages 1-7).

4. **Powder bridging, rat-holing, and screw coating**: Cohesive powders may bridge across the hopper outlet or rat-hole, intermittently starving the screw. Powder adhering to screw flights reduces effective flight volume (engisch2014lossinweightfeedingin pages 54-70).

5. **Moisture uptake**: For hygroscopic powders such as NaCl, moisture absorption increases bulk density, particle adhesion, and cohesion, all of which alter flow behavior. While not explicitly isolated in the studies reviewed, it is a well-known confound in pharmaceutical powder handling.

6. **Material buildup and headload variation**: Winski (2001) identifies material buildup on screw flights and headload variability as contributors to feeding performance drift (winski2001addressingfeedingperformance pages 2-3).

### Feed-Factor-vs-Fill-Level Calibration Practice

Pharmaceutical loss-in-weight feeder practice uses feed-factor profiles plotted against normalized hopper fill level. Bostijn et al. (2019) define FF_max (maximum feed factor) and FF_decay (the fill level at which FF drops to 90% of FF_max) as key material-specific response variables (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 6-10, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 10-14). The displacement-feed-factor concept of Fathollahi et al. (2020) tracks density variation during feeding via a material-specific curve that can be used to calibrate the system for accurate, constant feed rate (fathollahi2020performanceevaluationof pages 1-2). For this rig, the recommended practice is to measure or estimate cumulative dispensed mass as a proxy for fill-level depletion and to fit log(φ) against this covariate, making the 1.5–2× drift an explicitly modeled, predictable effect rather than unexplained noise.

## Q5. Tooling and a Portable Protocol

### Recommended Open-Source JAX Implementations

- **MAP optimization**: `optax` (gradient-based optimizers), `jaxopt` or `optimistix` (constrained optimization, Levenberg–Marquardt). These provide L-BFGS, Adam, and trust-region methods suitable for MAP fitting with autodiff gradients.
- **Differentiable ODEs**: `diffrax` for differentiable ODE/SDE integration in JAX, supporting event handling and adaptive stepping. Matei et al. (2025) demonstrate JAX/diffrax-based differentiable simulation through event-driven DAEs (matei2605differentiableparameteroptimization pages 1-2, matei2605differentiableparameteroptimization pages 2-4).
- **Differentiable Kalman filters and parameter learning**: `dynamax` provides JAX-native Kalman filtering, smoothing, and marginal-likelihood computation with automatic differentiation for parameter learning (linderman2025dynamaxapython pages 1-2, linderman2025dynamaxapython pages 2-4). It supports both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian inference for linear Gaussian state-space models.
- **Bayesian posterior sampling**: `numpyro` for probabilistic programming with NUTS/HMC and automatic Laplace approximation; `blackjax` for composable low-level MCMC/HMC/NUTS samplers in JAX (linderman2025dynamaxapython pages 1-2). Both are well-suited for sampling the posterior over 2–5 parameters given a differentiable log-density.
- **Whitehead group code**: `tsunamibayes` (GitHub) implements the random-walk Metropolis MCMC pipeline with GeoClaw forward models (ringer2021methodologicalreconstructionof pages 1-2, wonnacott2024methodologicalreconstructionof pages 7-9). Its architecture—explicit prior/likelihood specification with MCMC sampling over a modular forward model—is directly transferable to the doser, though the forward model would be replaced by the compartment model.

### Pitfalls of Differentiating Through Hybrid/Discontinuous Dynamics

The doser's start/stop dynamics, threshold-triggered halts, and Poisson-like clump arrivals create several challenges for automatic differentiation:

1. **Event-dependent gradients**: AD through hybrid dynamics produces gradients valid only for the particular event sequence selected by the forward simulation. If parameter changes alter the number, identity, or ordering of events (e.g., whether an arch breaks during or after a halt), the gradient becomes unreliable (matei2605differentiableparameteroptimization pages 1-2, matei2605differentiableparameteroptimization pages 2-4).

2. **Non-transversal crossings and grazing contacts**: Near event boundaries, gradients can be undefined or explosive. The standard remedy is to ensure transversal guard crossings and to segment the integration at event times (matei2605differentiableparameteroptimization pages 1-2, matei2605differentiableparameteroptimization pages 9-10).

3. **Discontinuous reset maps**: Halting the auger and triggering the tapper create state discontinuities. The discrete-adjoint approach treats these as equality constraints with Lagrange multipliers rather than penalizing them (matei2605differentiableparameteroptimization pages 9-10).

4. **Standard remedies**: (a) Use commanded rather than threshold-triggered stops in the calibration run to make halt times known inputs rather than functions of the estimated state. (b) Smooth hard switches with sigmoid or soft-max approximations (compliant-contact analogy) (newbury2024areviewof pages 10-11). (c) Use forward-mode AD (dual numbers) through event-handling code, which Rackauckas et al. (2021) show is robust and applicable to hybrid systems including event timing dependent on parameters (rackauckas2021acomparisonof pages 7-8). (d) Implement event-aware segmented integration with fixed scan lengths for JIT compatibility (matei2605differentiableparameteroptimization pages 2-4). (e) For stochastic clump arrivals, marginalize over the arrival process in the likelihood rather than trying to differentiate through random discrete events.

### Proposed "Calibrate a New Powder" Protocol and Parameter Card

**Minimal protocol** (10–15 minutes including loading):
1. Load powder into the tube-hopper assembly using a standardized fill procedure; record fill mass if feasible.
2. Measure bulk density, tapped density (Hausner ratio), and optionally d₅₀ of the powder.
3. Execute the multi-segment calibration run (6–10 segments, 3 RPM levels, varied durations, fixed tilt and tapping).
4. Run the MAP fit (φ first, then conditionally AF₀ and τ_af) with the stored population prior and a robust likelihood.
5. Compute profile likelihoods for each parameter; reject or pool parameters with non-identifiable profiles.
6. Store the parameter card.

**Per-powder parameter card contents**:
- Material identifier, lot, date, operator, environmental conditions (temperature, humidity)
- Measured material properties: bulk density, tapped density, Hausner ratio, d₅₀, moisture content
- Feed-factor estimate φ̂ (g/rev) with 95% posterior/profile CI at reference tilt and fill level
- Afterflow parameters AF₀ (mg) and τ_af (s) with CIs, or statement "not identifiable from this run"
- Process-noise and observation-noise scale estimates
- Fill-level covariate: initial fill, estimated fill at calibration, decay slope if measured
- Validity range: RPM range, tilt angle, fill-level range, time since calibration
- Re-calibration trigger: flag if cumulative dispensed mass exceeds X, or if closed-loop dose errors exceed 2σ of the stored posterior prediction, or if elapsed time exceeds the prior drift horizon

**Precedent**: Bostijn et al. (2019) demonstrate transferable powder characterization via a multivariate material-property database linked to feeder performance predictions (bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 6-10, bostijn2019amultivariateapproach pages 1-6). Li (2020) shows conditioned bulk density alone predicts feed factor with R² > 0.9 (li2020predictiveperformanceof pages 49-53). Van Snick et al. (2018, cited in Bostijn) built a multivariate raw-material-property database for pharmaceutical continuous manufacturing.

### Summary Verdict

The proposal to fit (φ, AF₀, τ_af) from a single run using autodiff MAP with a Gaussian prior is sound in principle and is equivalent to strong-constraint 4D-Var with a background term (ebtehaj2013onvariationaldownscaling pages 20-22, frion2026addaamodular pages 4-5, freitag2013synergyofinverse pages 1-4). However, it should be implemented with three modifications grounded in the literature: (1) use a robust (non-Gaussian) residual model to handle granular jump noise, (2) verify Laplace uncertainty estimates against profile likelihoods before trusting them, and (3) treat stored values as session priors with growing variance rather than constants. The strongest production estimator is a differentiable Kalman-filter marginal likelihood that integrates out latent states, with offline HMC for validation. Online CDA-style parameter adaptation should be deferred until offline estimates prove stable and the single-sensor, hybrid-dynamics limitations are addressed. Making hopper fill level observable and modeling feed-factor-vs-fill is the single highest-impact hardware/modeling change for reducing the dominant 1.5–2× drift.

artifacts.artifact-00:
| Method | What it estimates | Uncertainty output | Handles jump noise? | Key assumption | Computational cost for one 30–120 s run | Recommendation for this rig |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Single-run MAP with autodiff + Gaussian prior** | Batch estimate of session-specific parameters such as \(\phi\), \(AF_0\), and \(\tau_{af}\); optionally initial latent inventories or a few nuisance parameters | Point estimate plus local Hessian/Laplace covariance. Trustworthy only when the posterior is approximately unimodal and quadratic; otherwise use profiles or sampling | **Not by itself.** Gaussian residuals will interpret slugs, arches, and omitted history effects as parameter changes. Use Student-\(t\), mixture/outlier likelihoods, or explicit process noise | Differentiable, sufficiently identifiable, approximately well-specified simulator; a deterministic simulator makes this strong-constraint 4D-Var/MAP, while latent model-error increments make it weak-constraint (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000033) | **Low:** seconds to minutes after JIT compilation for 2–4 parameters; multiple starts and profile scans add cost | **Build first as a baseline**, but fit \(\phi\) first and conditionally fit afterflow only with multiple informative halts. Store the result as a session posterior, not a permanent constant. Validate Laplace intervals against profile likelihood or HMC (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000060) |
| **Online CDA/nudging parameter learning (Whitehead-style)** | Parameters inferred online from persistent observed-state synchronization error; CHL is Newton-like, while Gauss–Newton/Levenberg–Marquardt better handles correlated multiple parameters | Primarily trajectories and convergence diagnostics, **not inherently a calibrated posterior** | **Weakly.** Demonstrated numerically under noisy, sparse observations and stochastic forcing, but impulsive granular arrivals violate the smooth synchronization-error picture unless robustified (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000006) | Dissipative dynamics; observations and nudging sufficient for synchronization; a relaxed quasi-steady mismatch that remains informative and nondegenerate. Multiple parameters require independent sensitivity directions (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000008) | **Low to moderate:** one online model plus sensitivities; cheaper asymptotic sensitivities are available (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010) | **Defer as the primary calibrator.** Useful later as a lightweight within-dose adaptation or change detector for \(\phi\), but the single lagged scalar sensor, hybrid stops, short record, and afterflow history violate its strongest assumptions. Do not use its update trajectory as posterior uncertainty |
| **Dual or augmented-state UKF** | Sequential latent states and slowly varying parameters; augmented UKF retains state–parameter cross-covariance, while dual UKF uses separate state and parameter filters | Recursive Gaussian mean/covariance, but covariance is only calibrated if process/measurement models and tuning are credible | **Partly.** Ordinary UKF is Gaussian and vulnerable to clumps/outliers; robust innovations, Student-\(t\)/mixture updates, covariance inflation, or switching models are needed | Locally Gaussian, sufficiently smooth dynamics; parameters must be persistently excited. Dual filtering neglects explicit state–parameter cross-covariance; augmented filtering is more coupled but costlier (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052) | **Very low:** real time at 5 Hz for this small state; tuning and validation dominate compute | **Use for online control**, especially adaptive \(\phi\) with a conservative random walk, but estimate at most one or two parameters per dose. Keep \(AF_0\) and \(\tau_{af}\) fixed or slowly updated unless a calibration sequence supplies several informative halts |
| **Full Bayesian posterior with HMC/MCMC** | Joint posterior over parameters, latent states/inventories, noise scales, drift, and possibly discrete regimes or competing afterflow models | **Best available uncertainty characterization** if likelihood and model are adequate; reveals skewness, multimodality, boundaries, and parameter compensation | **Yes, when modeled explicitly.** Robust likelihoods, stochastic latent arrivals, mixture regimes, and model discrepancy can be included; Gaussian errors alone remain inadequate | A computable likelihood or differentiable log density and meaningful priors; posterior diagnostics and multiple chains are essential. Whitehead’s tsunami work illustrates explicit prior/likelihood assumptions and MCMC over uncertain, expensive forward models (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000017) | **Moderate:** minutes to hours for a low-dimensional differentiable model; random-walk MCMC is slower, whereas HMC/NUTS can exploit gradients | **Use offline as the uncertainty benchmark**, not in the dosing loop. Run it on selected calibration sessions and digital-twin cases to test MAP/Laplace coverage, detect ridges, and compare history-dependent afterflow models. It is the most trustworthy option only if jump noise and model discrepancy are represented |
| **Differentiable Kalman-filter marginal likelihood** | Static or session-level parameters learned by maximizing or sampling the innovation likelihood after analytically integrating linear-Gaussian latent states; can learn \(\phi\), lag/noise terms, and process-noise scales | MAP/ML Hessian, bootstrap, or full posterior over parameters; filter/smoother supplies latent-state covariance | **Better than deterministic least squares, but not automatically.** Process noise absorbs ordinary fluctuations; robust or switching observation/process models are still needed for slugs and arches | Conditional linear-Gaussian or acceptably approximated state-space model with credible covariance structure. The objective sums predictive innovation log likelihoods and can be differentiated end-to-end (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000068) | **Low:** roughly linear in 150–600 frames and very small state dimension; seconds after compilation | **Best first production estimator.** It respects balance lag and latent-flow uncertainty, avoids fitting a deterministic path to stochastic arrivals, and supports MAP first followed by HMC. Extend with robust innovations or an IMM; confirm identifiability with profiles and digital-twin coverage tests |


*Table: Comparison of five candidate estimators for session-level feed-factor and afterflow calibration, emphasizing uncertainty calibration, jump-noise robustness, assumptions, and computational burden. The strongest practical sequence is differentiable filter likelihood or robust MAP first, followed by offline posterior sampling for validation.*
